config.title: Third Reich Sites in Berlin - FAQ

items.q: What Third Reich sites can you actually visit in Berlin?
items.a: **The eleven worth knowing about are the Topography of Terror, the Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe, the Führerbunker car park, Bebelplatz, the former Reich Aviation Ministry, the German Resistance Memorial Center at the Bendlerblock, Gleis 17 at Grunewald, the House of the Wannsee Conference, Olympiastadion, Tempelhof Airport and Sachsenhausen.** They split into two very different kinds of visit: places that kept the original building and explain almost nothing, and places where nothing survived but the exhibition does all the work.

items.q: Can you visit Hitler's bunker in Berlin?
items.a: **No. The site is a residents' car park on In den Ministergärten, about five minutes from the Brandenburg Gate, and nothing of the bunker is visible.** There is a single information board, unveiled on 8 June 2006 in German and English, with a plan of the rooms. It is the only marker. Go if you are already walking between the Holocaust Memorial and Potsdamer Platz, and give it four minutes.

items.q: Is the Topography of Terror free?
items.a: **Yes, admission is free and there is no booking.** It opens daily from 10:00 to 20:00, and the outdoor areas close at dusk, never later than 20:00. You get the excavated cellar walls of the Gestapo and SS headquarters, roughly 200 metres of the outer Berlin Wall above them, an open-air exhibition along the trench and an indoor documentation centre. Allow about ninety minutes.

items.q: Are there any original Nazi buildings left in Berlin?
items.a: **Several, and the largest one in the centre is in daily government use.** The Reich Aviation Ministry on Wilhelmstraße, built for Hermann Göring between February 1935 and August 1936, is completely intact and is now the Federal Ministry of Finance, so you can only see the outside. Tempelhof's terminal by the same architect is also intact, the Olympiastadion still stands and still hosts football, and the villa at Wannsee is the actual house where the conference was held.

items.q: Which Third Reich sites in Berlin are free?
items.a: **Almost all of them.** Free with no ticket: the Topography of Terror, the Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe including its underground Information Centre, Bebelplatz, the German Resistance Memorial Center, Gleis 17, the House of the Wannsee Conference and the Sachsenhausen Memorial. The exceptions are Olympiastadion at **€11 for an adult self-guided visit** and the Tempelhof building, which is only reachable on a booked guided tour. The Tempelhof airfield itself is a free public park.

items.q: How long do you need at Sachsenhausen from Berlin?
items.a: **Half a day minimum, and I would leave the evening free afterwards.** The S1 takes about 45 minutes from Friedrichstraße, or the RE5 gets you to Oranienburg in about 25 minutes from Hauptbahnhof, then it is a 20 minute walk or the 804 bus. You need a zone ABC ticket. Admission is free. The grounds and exhibitions open 08:30 to 18:00 from 31 March to 26 October and 08:30 to 16:30 in winter.

items.q: Can you see the main Third Reich sites in Berlin in one day?
items.a: **The central ones, yes, and comfortably on foot.** Topography of Terror at 10:00 for ninety minutes, ten minutes at the old Aviation Ministry on Wilhelmstraße, four minutes at the bunker car park, then the Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe including an hour in the Information Centre below, lunch at Potsdamer Platz and the German Resistance Memorial Center in the afternoon. **Avoid a Monday**, because the Information Centre under the stelae is closed. Wannsee and Sachsenhausen do not fit into that day and need their own.

items.q: What are the rules about photos and behaviour at these sites?
items.a: **Keep your voice down, keep the phone away at the memorials, and photograph the place instead of yourself in it.** Climbing or posing on the stelae at the Holocaust Memorial is the thing that most upsets staff and other visitors. Beyond etiquette there is a legal line: **Nazi symbols and salutes are criminal offences in Germany**, including as a joke for a photograph, and people are arrested for it in Berlin every year.
